Daniel’s central move—treating Bell-inequality violation as an artifact of “curved” \( \sin^2(\theta/2) \) and proposing an \(L_1\) (Manhattan) geometry to “linearize” it—conflates a choice of *metric* with the *probability structure* that Bell constrains. Bell/CHSH inequalities are not derived from Euclidean distance; they follow from locality + realism + a very weak assumption that measurement outcomes are functions of a shared hidden variable and the chosen setting. The “settings” can be labeled any way you like; what matters is the pattern of correlations. In quantum mechanics those correlations come from the Hilbert-space inner product and the Born rule (an \(L_2\) structure), and the resulting limit is Tsirelson’s bound—not because space is “crooked,” but because the theory’s state space is. So an “\(L_1\) world” that restores local hidden variables wouldn’t be a mere re-metrization of the same physics; it would amount to changing the underlying state space and probability calculus (i.e., leaving standard quantum theory), which is a much stronger claim than the post acknowledges. A useful way to sharpen Daniel’s idea would be to frame it explicitly in the language of *generalized probabilistic theories*—where altering the geometry of the state space can indeed change attainable correlations, including super-quantum ones—rather than in terms of Manhattan distance on everyday space; see the standard discussion around PR-box correlations in [Popescu–Rohrlich (1994)](https://journals.aps.org/foundations-of-physics/abstract/10.1007/BF00736024).

A related blind spot is that “\( \pi=4\)” and “piecewise linear sin/cos” are properties of *taxicab geometry* definitions, not consequences of swapping a metric while keeping the rest of the physical and mathematical apparatus intact. One can define a “circle” via an \(L_1\) norm and get perimeter 8 for a unit “circle,” but Bell experiments don’t measure circumference; they measure joint outcome statistics across settings. If Daniel means “replace the Bloch sphere (an \(L_2\) object) with an \(L_1\)-ball state space,” then the post should say so—and then it owes the reader a statement of what replaces the Born rule and why the resulting theory still matches the many experiments that test Bell inequalities. Finally, a smaller but telling example: “triangle wave is pure tone” is false in ordinary Fourier analysis; a triangle wave contains infinitely many odd harmonics with amplitudes falling like \(1/n^2\). If the claim is meant “in an \(L_1\) harmonic analysis,” that again signals Daniel is really proposing a different analytic/probabilistic framework, not merely a different notion of distance.
